prompt: What products form when HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene (not counting cis–trans isomers)?

choices.why: Conjugated dienes give mixtures. Along with the Markovnikov 1,2 adduct, the 1,4 adduct 1-bromo-2-butene also forms.
The 1,2 adduct, 3-bromo-1-butene, forms too; it is the major product (71%) in the section's example.
4-Bromo-1-butene would need a primary, nonallylic carbocation, which doesn't form. The second product is the 1,4 adduct, 1-bromo-2-butene.

explanation: HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene to give a mixture: 3-bromo-1-butene (71%), the typical Markovnikov product of 1,2-addition, and 1-bromo-2-butene (29%), the product of 1,4-addition.

prompt: In the 1,4-addition of HBr to 1,3-butadiene, where do H and Br end up, and where is the remaining double bond?

choices.text: H and Br on carbons 1 and 4; the double bond between carbons 2 and 3
H and Br on carbons 1 and 2; the double bond between carbons 3 and 4
choices.why: That is 1,2-addition, which gives 3-bromo-1-butene.

choices.text: H and Br on carbons 1 and 4; no double bond remains
choices.why: Only one HBr adds, so one double bond remains. It moves to the middle of the chain, between carbons 2 and 3.

choices.text: H and Br on carbons 1 and 4; the double bond stays between carbons 1 and 2
choices.why: Carbon 1 becomes sp3 when an atom adds to it. The remaining double bond moves to between carbons 2 and 3.

explanation: In 1-bromo-2-butene, HBr has added to carbons 1 and 4 and the double bond has moved to a position between carbons 2 and 3. This result is described as 1,4-addition.

prompt: In the section's example, HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene to give 71% 3-bromo-1-butene. What percent of the product is the 1,4 adduct, 1-bromo-2-butene?
explanation: The two adducts make up the whole mixture: 100% − 71% = 29% 1-bromo-2-butene, the 1,4 adduct.

prompt: What does Br2 give when it adds to 1,3-butadiene at 20 °C?

choices.why: Like HBr, Br2 gives a mixture: the 1,4 adduct, 1,4-dibromo-2-butene (45%), forms along with the 1,2 adduct.
The 1,2 adduct, 3,4-dibromo-1-butene, also forms; it is the slightly larger part of the mixture (55%).
These names have no double bond. Adding one Br2 to a diene leaves one double bond in each product.

explanation: Many electrophiles besides HBr add to conjugated dienes to give mixtures. Br2 adds to 1,3-butadiene at 20 °C to give 3,4-dibromo-1-butene (55%, 1,2-addition) and 1,4-dibromo-2-butene (45%, 1,4-addition).

prompt: Br2 adds to 1,3-butadiene at 20 °C to give a 55 : 45 mixture of 1,2 and 1,4 adducts. If the reaction gives 12.0 g of dibromobutenes, how many grams are 1,4-dibromo-2-butene?
explanation: 1,4-Dibromo-2-butene is the 1,4 adduct, 45% of the mixture: 0.45 × 12.0 g = 5.4 g. The other 6.6 g is the 1,2 adduct, 3,4-dibromo-1-butene.

prompt: When H+ adds to 1,3-butadiene, why does it form a secondary allylic carbocation rather than a primary nonallylic one?

choices.text: The allylic cation is stabilized by resonance, so it is more stable and forms faster
Primary carbocations are more stable than secondary carbocations
choices.why: The reverse is true, and here the secondary cation is also allylic and resonance-stabilized.

choices.text: Br− adds first and directs H+ to carbon 1
choices.why: The electrophile H+ adds first. Br− bonds to the carbocation afterward.

choices.text: The allylic cation keeps its charge on one carbon, which stabilizes it
choices.why: The allylic cation's charge is shared between two carbons by resonance; that sharing is what stabilizes it.

explanation: Protonation of 1,3-butadiene could give a primary nonallylic carbocation or a secondary allylic cation. Because an allylic cation ("allylic" means next to a double bond) is stabilized by resonance between two forms, it is more stable and forms faster.

prompt: Protonating 1,3-butadiene gives the allylic cation CH3CH+CH=CH2 ↔ CH3CH=CHCH2+. Where must Br− bond to give the 1,2 adduct, 3-bromo-1-butene?

choices.text: At the CH carbon next to the CH3 group

choices.why: Bonding there gives the 1,4 adduct, 1-bromo-2-butene (BrCH2CH=CHCH3).
The CH3 carbon carries no positive charge. The charge is shared by the CH carbon next to it and the terminal CH2 carbon.

choices.text: At the central carbon of the three-carbon allylic unit
choices.why: The central carbon of the allylic unit bears no positive charge. Br− bonds at one of the two ends.

explanation: The positive charge is shared by the two ends of the allylic unit. Br− at the CH carbon next to CH3 gives CH3CHBrCH=CH2, 3-bromo-1-butene (the 1,2 adduct); Br− at the terminal CH2 gives BrCH2CH=CHCH3, 1-bromo-2-butene (the 1,4 adduct). The CH carbon is the more positive one, so the 1,2 product predominates (Figure 14.2.1).

prompt: What product forms when the nonconjugated diene 1,4-pentadiene reacts with 2 equivalents of HCl?

choices.why: That would be non-Markovnikov addition at both double bonds. Each HCl adds through the more stable secondary carbocation, putting Cl on carbons 2 and 4.
Each double bond reacts on its own with Markovnikov regiochemistry, so both chlorines go to the more substituted carbons, 2 and 4.
1,4-Pentadiene is not conjugated, so no allylic cation forms. Each double bond adds HCl like an ordinary alkene.

explanation: In a nonconjugated diene the double bonds react independently, each with Markovnikov regiochemistry through the more stable carbocation. Two equivalents of HCl therefore convert 1,4-pentadiene into 2,4-dichloropentane.

prompt: HCl adds to 2-methyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene, which has its methyl group on carbon 2. Why is protonation of the double bond between carbons 1 and 2 (at carbon 1) more likely than protonation of the other double bond?

choices.text: It gives a tertiary allylic cation rather than a secondary allylic cation
It gives a secondary allylic cation rather than a tertiary one
choices.why: Secondary cations are less stable. Protonating carbon 1 puts the positive charge on carbon 2, which carries the methyl group, so that cation is tertiary.

choices.text: It gives a nonallylic cation, which is more stable
choices.why: Nonallylic cations lack resonance stabilization. Both modes of protonation give allylic cations; the favored one is tertiary.

choices.text: It gives a symmetrical cation whose two resonance forms are equivalent
choices.why: That describes protonation of the other double bond (carbons 3 and 4), which gives a less stable, secondary allylic cation.

explanation: Protonation at carbon 1 puts the positive charge on carbon 2, which bears the methyl group, giving a tertiary allylic cation. Protonation of the double bond between carbons 3 and 4 gives a symmetrical but secondary allylic cation, so the first mode is more likely (Worked Example 14.2.1).

prompt: In Worked Example 14.2.1, HCl adds to 2-methyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene. Protonating either end of the diene, then letting Cl− bond at either end of each allylic cation, gives at most four products. How many different compounds actually result?
explanation: Protonation at carbon 1 gives 3-chloro-3-methylcyclohexene (1,2 adduct) and 3-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene (1,4 adduct). Protonation at carbon 4 gives a symmetrical cation, so its 1,2 and 1,4 adducts are the same compound, 6-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene. That makes three products.

prompt: In the addition of HCl to 2-methyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene, which product is both the 1,2 adduct and the 1,4 adduct of the same carbocation?

choices.why: That is the 1,2 adduct of the tertiary allylic cation. Its 1,4 partner is a different compound, 3-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene.
That is the 1,4 adduct of the tertiary allylic cation. Its 1,2 partner is 3-chloro-3-methylcyclohexene.
Only one HCl adds, so every product keeps a double bond.

explanation: Protonating the double bond between carbons 3 and 4 gives a symmetrical allylic cation whose two resonance forms are equivalent. Cl− at either end gives the same compound, 6-chloro-1-methylcyclohexene (Worked Example 14.2.1).

prompt: One equivalent of HCl adds to 1,3-pentadiene, CH2=CHCH=CHCH3. Which 1,2 adduct predominates?

choices.why: That 1,2 adduct comes from protonating carbon 4, which gives an allylic cation with a primary end. Protonating carbon 1 gives a more stable cation that is secondary at both ends.
That is a 1,4 adduct, not a 1,2 adduct.
That would need H+ to add to carbon 3, giving a nonallylic cation. Protonation at an end of the diene gives an allylic cation instead.

explanation: Protonation at carbon 1 gives CH3CH+CH=CHCH3, an allylic cation that is secondary at both ends; protonation at carbon 4 gives a cation with a primary end. The more stable cation's 1,2 and 1,4 adducts are both 4-chloro-2-pentene, so 4-chloro-2-pentene predominates (Exercise 14.2.2).

prompt: When H+ adds to carbon 1 of 1,3-pentadiene, why are the 1,2 and 1,4 adducts with Cl− the same compound?

choices.text: The allylic cation, CH3CH+CH=CHCH3, has identical ends, so Cl− at either end gives 4-chloro-2-pentene
Only one resonance form of this cation exists, so Cl− can bond at only one carbon
choices.why: The cation has two resonance forms. They are equivalent because both ends of the allylic unit carry the same groups.

choices.text: The 1,4 adduct rearranges into the 1,2 adduct as soon as it forms
choices.why: No rearrangement is needed: both ends of the symmetrical allylic cation are the same.

choices.text: Cl− bonds to the central carbon of the allylic unit in both cases
choices.why: The central carbon carries no positive charge. Cl− bonds at an end, and here both ends are equivalent.

explanation: Protonating carbon 1 gives CH3CH+CH=CHCH3 ↔ CH3CH=CHCH+CH3. Both ends of the allylic unit are CH carbons bearing a CH3 group, so Cl− at either end gives CH3CHClCH=CHCH3, 4-chloro-2-pentene (Exercise 14.2.1).

prompt: One equivalent of HBr adds to 2,3-dimethyl-1,3-cyclohexadiene. What is the 1,4 adduct?

choices.why: That is the 1,2 adduct, formed when Br− bonds at the tertiary, methyl-bearing end of the allylic cation.
Br bonds at an end of the allylic unit, which in the 1,4 adduct is the carbon right next to the new double bond (carbon 3 of the product), not carbon 4.
Only one HBr adds, so the product keeps one double bond.

explanation: Protonation at carbon 1 gives a tertiary allylic cation shared by carbons 2 and 4. Br− at carbon 2 gives the 1,2 adduct, 6-bromo-1,6-dimethylcyclohexene; Br− at carbon 4 gives the 1,4 adduct, in which the double bond lies between the two methyl-bearing carbons: 3-bromo-1,2-dimethylcyclohexene (Exercise 14.2.3).

prompt: Which earlier reaction gives a product mixture like that from electrophilic addition to a conjugated diene, for a similar reason?

choices.text: NBS bromination of alkenes, which goes through an allylic radical
HCl addition to 2-methylpropene, which goes through a tertiary carbocation
choices.why: That gives a single Markovnikov product, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane. Its carbocation isn't allylic.

choices.text: Addition of 2 equivalents of HCl to 1,4-pentadiene
choices.why: That nonconjugated diene gives a single product, 2,4-dichloropentane.

choices.text: Radical chlorination of methane, which goes through a methyl radical
choices.why: A methyl radical isn't allylic, so its unpaired electron isn't shared between two carbons.

explanation: A similar product mixture was seen for NBS bromination of alkenes (Section 10.3). That reaction proceeds through an allylic radical, which, like the allylic cation, spreads its reactive site over two carbons, so the bromine can end up at either one.
